title: The Milkmaid
imageDescription: A kitchen maid in a yellow bodice and blue apron pours milk from a jug into a bowl on a table with bread, lit from a window on the left.

statements.text: It's small: 45.5 × 41 cm. Most visitors expect it to be far bigger.
statements.why: Vermeer painted it around 1658, when he was in his mid-twenties. Almost all his paintings are this intimate.

statements.text: It's nearly life-size. The woman is painted at her real height.
statements.why: The whole canvas is under half a metre tall.

statements.text: Vermeer painted it straight onto a kitchen wall in Delft, and it was cut out later.
statements.why: It's oil on canvas, painted in his studio.

rounds.prompt: Look at the blue of her apron.
rounds.hint: What made a blue like this in 1658?

statements.text: It's natural ultramarine, ground from lapis lazuli mined in Afghanistan. It was one of the most expensive pigments of its time.
statements.why: Vermeer used it far more freely than most painters could afford to.

statements.text: It's woad, a cheap plant dye grown in the fields around Delft.
statements.why: Woad was used to dye cloth. The paint here is ultramarine.

statements.text: The apron was green until a restorer painted it blue in 1908.
statements.why: Scientific analysis shows the ultramarine is Vermeer's own paint.

rounds.prompt: Now the bread and basket on the table.
rounds.hint: Why does the crust seem to sparkle?

statements.text: Vermeer dabbed on tiny dots of light paint, a technique often called pointillé.
statements.why: Up close the highlights break into separate dots. From a step back they read as light catching a crust.

statements.text: He pressed real breadcrumbs into the wet paint to give it texture.
The bread was added a century later by another artist to fill an empty table.
statements.why: The still life is Vermeer's, and part of the original design.

rounds.prompt: Down at the floor, by the wall.
rounds.hint: What was here before the little box?

statements.text: Scans show Vermeer first painted a large wicker basket here, then replaced it with this foot warmer.
statements.why: The box held a pot of hot coals to warm someone's feet. The tiles along the wall include a Cupid, which some read as a hint about love.

statements.text: The box is a mousetrap, a joke about how poor the household was.
statements.why: It's a foot warmer, a common item in Dutch homes.

statements.text: The box lid hides Vermeer's initials, a secret signature.
statements.why: There's no signature on the foot warmer.

rounds.hint: Where has it been since Vermeer?

statements.text: The Rijksmuseum bought it in 1908, and it has belonged to the museum in Amsterdam ever since.
statements.why: It has travelled only for a few rare loans abroad.

statements.text: It was stolen in 1971 and found two weeks later in a Brussels garage.
statements.why: You may be thinking of another Vermeer, The Love Letter, stolen while on loan in Brussels in 1971.

statements.text: Napoleon's troops took it to the Louvre, and it only came home in 1945.
statements.why: It stayed in Dutch private collections until 1908.
